expected_evidence: Geological: absence or non-replication of anomalous markers (platinum spikes, nanodiamonds, magnetic spherules, aciniform soot) at putative Younger Dryas boundary (YDB) layers across North American sites, or demonstration that reported markers are artifacts of methodology/contamination rather than cosmic in origin

Astronomical: lack of a confirmed impact crater or airburst structure of appropriate age/size; orbital-dynamics modeling showing the Taurid meteor stream complex could not plausibly have delivered a body large enough to trigger continental-scale extinction/climate disruption at ~10,950 BCE

Geological/stratigraphic: evidence that the Younger Dryas cooling onset is better explained by non-impact mechanisms (e.g., meltwater pulse disrupting AMOC circulation) independent of any extraterrestrial trigger

Material/archaeological: megafaunal bone assemblages and radiocarbon dating showing extinction was staggered over centuries/millennia rather than an abrupt synchronous die-off coincident with a single impact event, overlapping instead with human hunting (Clovis kill sites) and habitat/climate stress

Genetic: ancient DNA/population-genomic studies showing gradual population decline and bottleneck trajectories in megafauna beginning well before or continuing well after the proposed impact date, inconsistent with a single catastrophic triggering event

Model-prior (low-tier, unverified): recollection that a substantial body of post-2007 peer-reviewed literature (e.g., Pinter et al. 2011 'double falsification' review, failed independent replications of nanodiamond/platinum signatures) argued against the Younger Dryas Impact Hypothesis, though the debate remained contested and not fully settled as of training knowledge
response.rationale: This hypothesis dates to the Younger Dryas onset (~10,950 BCE), so the 'younger-dryas' detectability row is most applicable. The evidence needed to refute a cosmic-impact cause for North American megafaunal extinction is overwhelmingly geological (stratigraphic marker layers, crater/airburst absence: 0.65) and astronomical (orbital dynamics, impact physics constraints: 0.7) in nature, both of which score highly detectable in this period, since boundary sediment sequences and impact-diagnostic proxies (or their absence) are routinely preserved and are actively studied by modern geochemistry/stratigraphy regardless of the deep antiquity of the event itself. Supporting material (faunal/archaeological dating, 0.35) and genetic (ancient DNA population trajectories, 0.3) evidence is moderately detectable but more fragmentary. Textual (0.0), linguistic (0.05), oral_tradition (0.1), and iconographic (0.1) evidence are essentially irrelevant/undetectable for a purely geophysical refutation claim of this age, as no Upper Paleolithic/Younger Dryas society left written or securely interpretable symbolic records of such an event. Because the strongest and most diagnostic evidence classes (geological, astronomical) have comparatively high detectability in this period, an absence of confirmed impact markers or crater evidence is a meaningful, plausible signal rather than simply reflecting poor preservation — this refutation-type hypothesis could plausibly have been established through real paleoclimate/geochemical research. I weight the overall detectability adjustment toward these two high-detectability kinds since they are the primary evidentiary basis for such a refutation claim, while noting my knowledge of the actual state of YDIH debate literature is a low-tier model-prior recollection, not verified against the evidence text provided.
